questions.text: Which of the following anatomical features is a primary distinguishing characteristic of a pulmonary vein when compared to a pulmonary artery?
options: A thicker tunica media
Presence of internal valves to prevent backflow
A narrower lumen relative to wall thickness
The presence of a thick layer of elastic fibers
questions.explanation: Veins, including the pulmonary vein, typically have thinner muscular walls (tunica media) and larger lumens than arteries. A key feature of veins is the presence of internal semilunar valves that ensure one-way blood flow and prevent backflow under lower pressure.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: In the provided schematic of blood vessel cross-sections, which label represents the vessels where the exchange of nutrients and gases occurs, and what is its wall composition?
options: A; Thick muscular wall
B; Thin wall with valves
C; Single layer of endothelium only
A and B; Tunica externa and media
questions.explanation: Capillaries (represented by 'C') are the site of exchange between blood and interstitial fluid. To facilitate efficient diffusion, their walls consist only of a single layer of squamous epithelium called endothelium (tunica interna), lacking both the tunica media and tunica externa.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: In a healthy human adult, what is the standard range of time required for blood to undergo the normal clotting process at the site of a minor injury?
options: 1-2 minutes
4-10 minutes
15-20 minutes
1-2 hours
questions.explanation: Normal blood clotting (coagulation) typically takes between 4 to 10 minutes in a healthy individual. This process involves a series of enzymatic reactions leading to the formation of a fibrin mesh.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text:
Match the blood groups in Column I with their correct clinical description in Column II:

| Column I (Blood Group) | Column II (Description) |
| :--- | :--- |
| I. Group O | P. Universal Recipient |
| II. Group AB | Q. Universal Donor |
| III. Group A | R. Contains Anti-B antibodies |
options: I-P, II-Q, III-R
I-Q, II-P, III-R
I-R, II-P, III-Q
I-Q, II-R, III-P
questions.explanation: Blood group O is the universal donor because it lacks A and B antigens on RBCs. Blood group AB is the universal recipient because it lacks anti-A and anti-B antibodies in the plasma. Group A has anti-B antibodies.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: Which of the following pregnancy scenarios poses the highest risk for the development of erythroblastosis foetalis in the second child if no medical intervention (like anti-Rh antibodies) is provided?
options: Rh+ve mother and Rh-ve foetus
Rh-ve mother and Rh-ve foetus
Rh-ve mother and Rh+ve foetus
Rh+ve mother and Rh+ve foetus
questions.explanation: Erythroblastosis foetalis occurs when an Rh-ve mother is sensitized to Rh+ve blood (usually during the first delivery of an Rh+ve child). In subsequent pregnancies with an Rh+ve foetus, the mother's Rh antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the foetal RBCs.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: In humans, blood platelets (thrombocytes) are unique cellular fragments. Which of the following statements correctly identifies their origin and characteristic?
options: They are nucleated cells that originate from lymphocytes.
They are larger than RBCs and originate from monocytes.
They are non-nucleated fragments produced from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow.
They are biconcave cells that lack hemoglobin and originate from the spleen.
questions.explanation: Platelets are not true cells but are non-nucleated protoplasmic discs or fragments produced from very large cells called megakaryocytes in the bone marrow. They play a critical role in blood clotting by releasing thromboplastin.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: Refer to the provided schematic of double circulation. Identify vessel 'P' and its primary physiological role.
options: Pulmonary vein; carrying oxygenated blood from lungs to the heart
Systemic artery; carrying oxygenated blood to body tissues
Pulmonary artery; carrying deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs
Vena cava; carrying deoxygenated blood from body tissues to the heart
questions.explanation: In the double circulation schematic, 'P' represents the pulmonary artery. Unlike most arteries, it carries deoxygenated blood away from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation.

questions.text:
Study the table of human physiological parameters and select the option that correctly identifies the average values for a healthy adult at rest:

| Parameter | Average Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| A. Normal Heart Rate | 72–75 beats per minute |
| B. Normal Breathing Rate | 12–16 times per minute |
| C. RBC Lifespan | 120 days |
| D. Blood Clotting Time | 4–10 minutes |
options: Only A and B are correct
A, B, and C are correct
B, C, and D are correct
All (A, B, C, and D) are correct
questions.explanation: All the listed physiological parameters are standard clinical averages for a healthy adult human: heart rate (approx. 75 bpm), breathing rate (12-16/min), RBC lifespan (120 days), and clotting time (4-10 min).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: Double circulation ensures the complete separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Based on the conduction system schematic, which structure initiates the cardiac cycle to maintain this rhythmic flow in birds and mammals?
options: Label A (SA node)
Label B (AV node)
Label C (Bundle of His)
Label D (Purkinje fibers)
questions.explanation: In mammals and birds, the heart is completely divided into four chambers. The rhythmic contraction is initiated by the Sinoatrial (SA) node, labelled 'A', which acts as the primary pacemaker of the heart.
questions.subject: Biology
questions.image_alt: Schematic of the heart's conduction system with labels A at the top of the right atrium, B at the junction, C in the septum, and D in the ventricular walls.

questions.text: The arterial blood pressure is not constant during the cardiac cycle. At which specific point is the maximum pressure exerted against the arterial walls?
options: During atrial systole
During ventricular diastole
During ventricular systole, as blood enters the aorta
During the joint diastole phase
questions.explanation: Blood pressure is highest during ventricular systole (systolic pressure) when the left ventricle contracts and forcibly ejects blood into the aorta. It is lowest during ventricular diastole (diastolic pressure).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: During the 'Joint Diastole' phase of the cardiac cycle, which of the following describes the state of the chambers and valves?
options: All chambers are contracted; all valves are open.
Atria are contracted; AV valves are closed; semilunar valves are open.
Ventricles are contracted; semilunar valves are open; AV valves are closed.
All four chambers are relaxed; AV valves are open; semilunar valves are closed.
questions.explanation: In joint diastole, all four chambers (atria and ventricles) are in a relaxed state. The tricuspid and bicuspid (AV) valves are open, allowing blood to flow from the veins into the ventricles, while the semilunar valves are closed to prevent backflow from the great arteries.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: Lymph plays a vital role in the body's transport and defense systems. Which of the following is a specialized function of lymph in the digestive system?
options: Transporting oxygen to the intestinal mucosal cells
Absorption of dietary fats via lacteals in the intestinal villi
Producing digestive enzymes in the lymph nodes
Directly filtering nitrogenous wastes from the hepatic portal vein
questions.explanation: Lymph (chyle) is responsible for the absorption and transport of dietary fats and fat-soluble vitamins. This occurs in specialized lymphatic capillaries called lacteals located within the villi of the small intestine.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: In the mammalian heart, what is the specific function of the chordae tendinae?
options: To contract and push blood from the atria into the ventricles
To prevent the tricuspid and bicuspid valves from everting into the atria during ventricular contraction
To relay electrical impulses from the SA node to the AV node
To provide structural support to the thick walls of the left ventricle
questions.explanation: Chordae tendinae are tough, fibrous cords ('heart strings') that connect the flaps of the AV valves (tricuspid and bicuspid) to the papillary muscles. They prevent the valve flaps from being forced upward or 'inside out' into the atria when ventricular pressure rises during systole.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: Simple aquatic organisms like sponges and coelenterates lack a dedicated circulatory system. How do they facilitate the exchange of nutrients and wastes for their cells?
options: By using a high-pressure open circulatory system with hemolymph
By circulating water from the surrounding environment through their body cavities
By relying entirely on active transport across a thick chitinous skin
By using specialized migratory cells that carry nutrients like blood
questions.explanation: Sponges and coelenterates use water from their environment as a circulating medium. They move water through their body cavities (like the spongocoel or gastrovascular cavity), allowing individual cells to directly exchange nutrients, gases, and wastes.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: During the initial stages of the blood coagulation cascade at a site of injury, which component is responsible for the release of thromboplastin (thrombokinase)?
options: Damaged erythrocytes
Activated lymphocytes
Disintegrated blood platelets
Plasma albumin proteins
questions.explanation: When an injury occurs, platelets (thrombocytes) at the site disintegrate and release thromboplastin. This enzyme (also known as thrombokinase) is essential for initiating the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin in the presence of calcium ions.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text:
Match the heart valves and structures with their anatomical descriptions:

| Structure | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| 1. Bicuspid (Mitral) Valve | X. Guarding the right atrio-ventricular opening |
| 2. Tricuspid Valve | Y. Guarding the left atrio-ventricular opening |
| 3. Chordae Tendinae | Z. Fibrous threads connecting valves to papillary muscles |
questions.explanation: The bicuspid or mitral valve is located between the left atrium and left ventricle. The tricuspid valve is between the right atrium and right ventricle. Both are tethered by chordae tendinae to prevent eversion.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: In the provided double circulation schematic, which vessel is represented by label 'S', and what is the oxygenation state of the blood it carries?
options: Pulmonary artery; Deoxygenated
Pulmonary vein; Oxygenated
Systemic artery; Oxygenated
Venae cavae; Deoxygenated
questions.explanation: Label 'S' represents the venae cavae (superior and inferior). These vessels collect deoxygenated blood from the systemic body tissues and deliver it back to the right atrium of the heart.

questions.text:
Erythrocytes (RBCs) from different species vary in shape and lifespan. Based on the data and the protein schematic, which of the following is correct?

| Species | RBC Shape | RBC Nucleus | Average Lifespan |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Human | Biconcave | Absent | 120 days |
| Frog | Biconvex | Present | 100 days |
| Rabbit | Biconcave | Absent | 80 days |
options: The RBC with the highest hemoglobin concentration (Human) has the shortest lifespan.
A molecule of adult human hemoglobin, found in these cells, consists of 574 amino acids total.
Rabbit RBCs are nucleated and live longer than human RBCs.
Frog RBCs are biconcave and lack the respiratory pigment shown in the diagram.
questions.explanation: Adult human hemoglobin is a tetramer consisting of two alpha chains (141 AA each) and two beta chains (146 AA each), totaling 574 amino acids ($2 \times 141 + 2 \times 146 = 574$). The table correctly shows that humans have the longest RBC lifespan among these three, while rabbits have the shortest (80 days).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: When a whole blood sample is centrifuged, it separates into two primary layers 'P' and 'Q' as shown. Which layer contains the 'buffy coat' and what is the approximate volume percentage of fraction 'Q'?
questions.explanation: Centrifugation separates blood into plasma (P, approx. 55%) and formed elements (Q, approx. 45%). Layer Q includes the erythrocytes at the bottom and a thin white 'buffy coat' containing leukocytes and platelets just above them.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.text: The autonomic nervous system regulates heart activity. How do neural signals from the sympathetic nerves specifically influence the heart, according to the conduction schematic?
options: They inhibit label A to decrease the heart rate.
They stimulate label A to increase heart rate and increase the strength of ventricular contraction.
They bypass labels A and B to act only on label D to slow the heart down.
They stimulate label B only, with no effect on the overall rate.
questions.explanation: Sympathetic neural signals increase both the rate of heartbeat (by acting on the SA node, label 'A') and the force/strength of ventricular contraction, thereby increasing the total cardiac output. Parasympathetic signals have the opposite effect.
